transcript.text: Tom, Zara, you've written up the sleep experiment. How many people took part again?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: We recruited them through posters in the library and the sports centre, and offered a small payment for taking part.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Fine. Was there any problem with people dropping out?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Only a few, mostly because of exams. We replaced them quickly, so the groups stayed balanced.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: Sixty, aged between eighteen and thirty. All of them students.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: Good. Walk me through the procedure.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Before we started, every participant signed a consent form, and we explained that they could stop at any time.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: Good. Ethics always need to be clear in the methods section.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Sure. Participants first filled in a diary about their daily habits for two weeks.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Then each person wore a wristband that records movement during the night.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: After that, half of them stopped using phones in bed, while the others carried on as normal.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: At the end, everybody took a memory test, so we could compare results.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: How did you make sure the groups were comparable?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: We divided them randomly, but we checked that the average age and daily routine were similar in both groups.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: That's an important step. Many studies forget to describe it properly.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Clear. What did you find? Start with sleep length.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: People without phones slept about twenty minutes longer, which is a small effect but consistent.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Mood improved clearly. They reported feeling calmer in the morning.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: The participants were quite honest about their feelings, which I think makes the results more reliable.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Self-reports can be tricky, but combining them with the wristband data is a strength.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: And memory?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Honestly, there was no change at all in the memory scores.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Concentration at work?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: That was mixed. Some people improved a lot, others got worse, probably because of stress at work.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: Age matters for weight changes, though. Younger participants lost a little weight, older ones didn't.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Interesting. Did the older participants differ in other ways too?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: Not really. Their sleep patterns were very similar, so we didn't draw any conclusions from it.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: And dreams?
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: We only asked about dreams at the end, so we can't say much. This needs more research with proper tools.
transcript.speaker: ZARA

transcript.text: Thank you. Revise the discussion section and I'll read it again on Wednesday.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN

transcript.text: We'll also add a short paragraph on the limitations, like the small number of participants.
transcript.speaker: TOM

transcript.text: Yes, please. Honesty about limitations is a sign of good research.
transcript.speaker: DR MORGAN
